notes.definition: Nanoparticles have many applications, including in medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts, mainly because of their high surface area to volume ratio. Their use has advantages but also possible risks to health and the environment that are not yet fully understood.
explanation: Nanoparticles are particles 1 to 100 nm across. Because of their very high surface area to volume ratio, they can have properties different from the same materials in bulk, and smaller quantities may be needed to be effective. These features have led to many applications, and developing new uses for nanoparticulate materials is an important area of research.

Applications include: medicine, for example nanoparticles that carry drugs to specific cells in the body, and silver nanoparticles in wound dressings that kill bacteria; electronics, where nanoparticles are used to make very small components and conductive inks; cosmetics and sun creams, where nanoparticles of substances such as titanium dioxide and zinc oxide give better skin coverage and more effective protection from ultraviolet (UV) light, without leaving a white layer on the skin; deodorants, where silver nanoparticles have antibacterial properties that reduce the bacteria that cause odour; and catalysts, where the huge surface area of nanoparticles means a smaller mass of catalyst is needed.

Each application has advantages. Less material may be needed, saving money and resources (important when the material is expensive, such as platinum or silver). Products can be more effective, for example a sun cream that protects better, or a catalyst that speeds up a reaction more. Nanoparticles can also make new products possible, such as clear sun creams or targeted medicines.

There are also possible risks. Because nanoparticles are so small, they may be absorbed through the skin, breathed into the lungs or taken into cells, where they could cause damage. Their high surface area may make them catalyse unwanted reactions in the body. Nanoparticles washed down drains, for example from clothing or sun cream, could harm organisms in the environment, such as useful bacteria. The long-term effects on health and the environment are not yet known, because these materials are new and not enough research has been done.

In the exam you may be given information about a specific use and asked to evaluate it. Evaluating means weighing up advantages and disadvantages using the information given, and then reaching a justified conclusion. You do not need to learn specific examples beyond those given in questions, but you should be able to explain that there are possible risks associated with nanoparticles, and why they arise from their small size and high surface area to volume ratio.
keyFacts: Nanoparticles are used in medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts.
Most uses depend on the high surface area to volume ratio of nanoparticles.
Smaller quantities of nanoparticles may be needed than of normal-sized particles.
Nanoparticles in sun creams give better skin coverage and protection from UV, and do not leave white marks.
Silver nanoparticles have antibacterial properties (deodorants, dressings, clothing).
Nanoparticle catalysts have a large surface area, so less catalyst is needed.
Possible risks: nanoparticles may be absorbed through skin, breathed in or enter cells and cause damage.
The long-term effects of nanoparticles on health and the environment are not yet fully known.
New applications of nanoparticles are an important area of research.

keyTerms.definition: A particle 1 to 100 nm in size with a very high surface area to volume ratio.
A practical use of a material or technology.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up. Nanoparticle catalysts have a large surface area.
Able to kill bacteria or stop them growing, as silver nanoparticles can.
The chance that a hazard will cause harm. Nanoparticles may pose risks because their effects are not fully known.
To judge something by weighing up advantages and disadvantages to reach a justified conclusion.

equations.name: Surface area to volume ratio
equations.formula: surface area to volume ratio = surface area ÷ volume
equations.symbols: SA : V = SA ÷ V (for a cube, 6 ÷ L)

workedExamples.title: Comparing catalyst particles
workedExamples.question: A catalyst is used as cubes of side 1000 nm or as nanoparticle cubes of side 10 nm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each and state how many times greater the nanoparticle value is.
steps: Large cubes: SA : V = 6 ÷ 1000 = 0.006 per nm.
workedExamples.answer: 0.006 and 0.6 per nm; the nanoparticles have a surface area to volume ratio 100 times greater, so much less catalyst is needed.

workedExamples.title: Converting a size
workedExamples.question: Silver nanoparticles in a sock have a diameter of 25 nm. Write this in metres.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating a use
workedExamples.question: Evaluate the use of silver nanoparticles in socks to prevent odour.
steps: Advantage: silver nanoparticles are antibacterial, so they kill the bacteria that cause odour.
Advantage: their high SA : V means only a small mass of silver is needed.
Disadvantage: nanoparticles may be washed out into waste water and could harm useful bacteria in the environment.
Disadvantage: possible absorption through the skin; long-term effects are not known.
Conclusion: they are effective, but the possible risks mean more research is needed before they are widely used.
workedExamples.answer: A balanced judgement that weighs effectiveness and small quantities against unknown health and environmental risks.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nanoparticles are completely safe because they are used in everyday products.
misconceptions.right: In fact their long-term effects on health and the environment are not yet fully known, so there are possible risks.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think nanoparticles are dangerous simply because they are 'chemicals'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the possible risks come specifically from their tiny size and high surface area to volume ratio, which may let them enter the body and cells, and react in unexpected ways.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think more nanoparticle material is needed because the particles are so small.
misconceptions.right: In fact smaller quantities are usually needed, because the high surface area to volume ratio makes them more effective per gram.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write a one-sided answer to 'evaluate' questions.
misconceptions.right: In fact evaluating requires both advantages and disadvantages, followed by a justified conclusion.

realWorld: Many sun creams contain nanoparticles of titanium dioxide or zinc oxide, which protect against UV light without leaving white marks.
Silver nanoparticles are used in some deodorants, sports clothing and wound dressings for their antibacterial properties.
Researchers are developing nanoparticles that deliver anti-cancer drugs directly to tumour cells, reducing side effects.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Chemistry (8462) only, not Combined Science.
Nanoparticles have applications in medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants and as catalysts.
Consider advantages and disadvantages of these applications, and evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose given information.
Explain that there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles.
examTips: In 'evaluate' questions, give at least one advantage and one disadvantage from the information, then a conclusion that says whether the use is a good idea and why.
Link advantages to 'high surface area to volume ratio' and 'smaller quantities needed'.
For risks, mention that nanoparticles could be absorbed into the body (skin, lungs, cells) and that long-term effects are not yet known.
Use only the data given in the question; you do not need to remember specific products.
Check units carefully when converting between nm and m: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m.
summary: Nanoparticles are used in medicine, electronics, cosmetics, sun creams, deodorants and catalysts.
Their high surface area to volume ratio makes them effective in small quantities.
Sun creams with nanoparticles give better coverage and UV protection without white marks.
Possible risks include absorption into the body and harm to the environment.
Long-term effects are not fully known, so evaluation and further research are needed.

flashcards.front: Name five areas where nanoparticles are used.
flashcards.back: Medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants, catalysts.
They have a high surface area to volume ratio, so less catalyst is needed.

flashcards.front: Why are nanoparticles used in sun creams?
flashcards.back: Better skin coverage and more effective UV protection, without leaving white marks.

flashcards.front: Why are silver nanoparticles used in deodorants?
flashcards.back: They are antibacterial: they kill the bacteria that cause odour.

flashcards.front: Give one medical use of nanoparticles.
flashcards.back: Targeted drug delivery, or antibacterial wound dressings.

flashcards.front: Give one use of nanoparticles in electronics.
flashcards.back: Very small components or conductive inks.
They may be absorbed through skin, breathed in or enter cells, and their long-term effects are unknown.

flashcards.front: How could nanoparticles harm the environment?
flashcards.back: When washed into waste water they could harm useful organisms, such as bacteria.

flashcards.front: What must you include in an 'evaluate' answer?
flashcards.back: Advantages, disadvantages and a justified conclusion.

flashcards.front: Why may smaller quantities of nanoparticles be needed?
flashcards.back: Their high surface area to volume ratio makes them effective in small amounts.

flashcards.front: Why are long-term risks of nanoparticles uncertain?
flashcards.back: They are relatively new materials, so not enough long-term research has been done.

questions.question: Which of these is a use of nanoparticles?
options: Sun creams
Building bricks
Copper water pipes
Glass windows
markScheme: 1 mark: Sun creams
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are used in sun creams to give better coverage and UV protection. The others are bulk materials.

questions.question: Silver nanoparticles are added to some deodorants. What property makes them useful?
options: They conduct electricity
They are antibacterial
They have a high melting point
They are magnetic
markScheme: 1 mark: They are antibacterial
questions.explanation: Silver nanoparticles kill bacteria, which reduces the bacteria that cause body odour.

questions.question: Why are nanoparticles useful as catalysts?
options: They have a low melting point
They are very heavy
They have a high surface area to volume ratio
They are coloured
markScheme: 1 mark: They have a high surface area to volume ratio
questions.explanation: Reactions on a catalyst happen at its surface, and nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio.

questions.question: Which is a possible risk of using nanoparticles in cosmetics?
options: They make the product too heavy
They could be absorbed through the skin and damage cells
They make the product a different colour
They make the product cost more to transport
markScheme: 1 mark: They could be absorbed through the skin and damage cells
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles are so small that they may pass through the skin and enter cells. Their long-term effects are not known.

questions.question: Why do sun creams containing nanoparticles not leave a white layer on the skin?
options: Nanoparticles are transparent on the skin because they are so small
Nanoparticles evaporate quickly
Nanoparticles are absorbed completely into the blood
Nanoparticles are coloured to match skin
markScheme: 1 mark: Nanoparticles are transparent on the skin because they are so small
questions.explanation: The particles are so small that the cream appears transparent, while still giving good coverage and UV protection.

questions.question: Why might a smaller mass of a nanoparticle catalyst be needed than of a powdered catalyst?
options: Nanoparticles are more dense
Nanoparticles are not used up
Nanoparticles provide more surface area per gram
Nanoparticles react with the products
markScheme: 1 mark: Nanoparticles provide more surface area per gram
questions.explanation: Higher surface area to volume ratio means more surface per gram, so less catalyst gives the same effect. All catalysts are not used up, so that is not the difference.

questions.question: Why are the long-term effects of nanoparticles on health not fully known?
options: Nanoparticles do not affect health
Nanoparticles are a relatively new technology and research is still being done
Nanoparticles cannot be studied in laboratories
Nanoparticles only exist for a few seconds
markScheme: 1 mark: Nanoparticles are a relatively new technology and research is still being done
questions.explanation: Nanotechnology is relatively new, so there has not been enough time to study long-term effects fully.

questions.question: Silver nanoparticles in clothing may be washed into waste water. What is the main environmental concern?
options: They could kill useful bacteria in the environment
They could make the water radioactive
They could make the water too acidic
They will turn into silver bars
markScheme: 1 mark: They could kill useful bacteria in the environment
questions.explanation: Silver nanoparticles are antibacterial, so if released they may also kill helpful bacteria, for example in sewage treatment.

questions.question: A company wants to replace 10 g of a powdered platinum catalyst with platinum nanoparticles. Which statement is the best evaluation?
options: Nanoparticles should not be used because platinum is a metal
Nanoparticles are always better and have no disadvantages
Nanoparticles should be used because platinum is cheap
Less platinum would be needed, saving money, but possible risks of handling nanoparticles should be considered
markScheme: 1 mark: Less platinum would be needed, saving money, but possible risks of handling nanoparticles should be considered
questions.explanation: A good evaluation weighs the advantage (high SA : V so less expensive platinum needed) against possible risks to workers and the environment.

questions.question: Why may nanoparticles cause harm inside the body when the same substance in bulk is harmless?
options: Nanoparticles contain different elements
Their small size lets them enter cells, and their high surface area may make them more reactive
They are radioactive
They are always toxic gases
markScheme: 1 mark: Their small size lets them enter cells, and their high surface area may make them more reactive
questions.explanation: The same substance can behave differently as nanoparticles: tiny size allows entry into cells and high SA : V can increase reactivity.

questions.question: In which area are nanoparticles used to carry drugs to specific cells?
options: Electronics
Construction
Medicine
Farming machinery
markScheme: 1 mark: Medicine
questions.explanation: In medicine, nanoparticles are being developed to deliver drugs to particular cells, such as cancer cells.

questions.question:
Silver nanoparticles in a wound dressing have a diameter of 20 nm.
Calculate the diameter of the nanoparticles in metres.
Give your answer in standard form.

A nanoparticle catalyst is made of cubes.
Figure 1 shows one of the cubes.
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of the cube.

markScheme: 1 mark: SA = 6 × 2² = 24 nm² and V = 2³ = 8 nm³
1 mark: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 per nm
questions.explanation: Surface area 24 nm² divided by volume 8 nm³ gives 3 per nm, which matches 6 ÷ L = 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

questions.question:
A sun cream contains 5% nanoparticles by mass.
Calculate the mass of nanoparticles in a 200 g bottle of the sun cream.

A factory uses 100 g of a powdered catalyst.
Table 1 shows the relative surface area per gram of two forms of the catalyst.
Calculate the mass of the nanoparticle catalyst that would give the same total surface area as 100 g of the powdered catalyst.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 2 g
questions.explanation: To provide the same surface area, you need 50 times less mass: 100 ÷ 50 = 2 g.

questions.question:
Titanium dioxide particles are used in sun creams.
Table 1 shows the side lengths of the particles in an old sun cream and in a new sun cream.
The particles are cubes.
Calculate the factor by which the surface area to volume ratio of the particles has increased.

headers: Side length of particles in nm

markScheme: 1 mark: SA : V old = 6 ÷ 3000 = 0.002 per nm; new = 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2 per nm
questions.explanation: The side has decreased by a factor of 100 (3000 ÷ 30), so SA : V increases by a factor of 100.

questions.question:
A process uses a platinum catalyst.
Table 1 shows information about two forms of the catalyst.
Calculate how much money is saved by using the nanoparticles instead of the powder.
markScheme: 1 mark: powder cost = 5.0 × 25 = £125; nanoparticle cost = 0.50 × 40 = £20
1 mark: saving = 125 − 20 = £105
questions.explanation: Although nanoparticles cost more per gram, far less is needed. £125 − £20 = £105 saved.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a cube of zinc oxide with sides of 1 μm (1000 nm).
The cube is divided into nanoparticle cubes with sides of 10 nm.
Calculate the number of nanoparticles made.

markScheme: 1 mark: 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 cubes along each edge
questions.explanation: Each edge is split into 100 pieces, so the number of cubes is 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 × 10⁶. A common error is to give 100.

questions.question: Give one use of nanoparticles in medicine.
markScheme: 1 mark: (targeted) drug delivery / antibacterial wound dressings
questions.explanation: Nanoparticles can carry drugs to specific cells or kill bacteria in wound dressings.

questions.question: State two advantages of using nanoparticles in sun creams.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: better skin coverage; more effective protection from UV light; does not leave white marks (transparent)
questions.explanation: These advantages come from the very small size and high surface area to volume ratio of the particles.

questions.question: Explain why there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles.
markScheme: 1 mark: because they are so small they may be absorbed through the skin / breathed in / enter cells (and cause damage)
1 mark: their long-term effects on health or the environment are not yet known
questions.explanation: Risks come from the tiny size of nanoparticles and the lack of long-term research.

Figure 1 shows a silver bar and the same mass of silver as nanoparticles.
Suggest why silver nanoparticles are more effective at killing bacteria than the same mass of a silver bar.

acceptedAnswers: high surface area to volume ratio
markScheme: 1 mark: nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
1 mark: so more silver is exposed / in contact with bacteria
questions.explanation: Most of the silver in a bar is inside, away from any bacteria. Nanoparticles expose a much larger proportion of their atoms.

questions.question: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using nanoparticles in deodorants.
markScheme: 1 mark: advantage, e.g. kill odour-causing bacteria / only small amounts needed
1 mark: disadvantage, e.g. may be absorbed through the skin / long-term effects unknown / may harm the environment when washed away
questions.explanation: A balanced answer gives one benefit (effectiveness) and one possible risk.

questions.question: A scientist says that new applications of nanoparticles should be tested for many years before being used in products. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: nanoparticles may have different properties from bulk material, so we cannot assume they are safe
1 mark: their long-term effects on health and the environment are not yet known
questions.explanation: Because nanoparticles can behave differently from the bulk material, safety data for the bulk substance may not apply.

questions.question: Name one other area, apart from medicine, in which nanoparticles are used.
markScheme: 1 mark: electronics / cosmetics / sun creams / deodorants / catalysts
questions.explanation: The AQA specification lists medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts.

questions.question:
Nanoparticles of titanium dioxide are used in sun creams.
Evaluate the use of nanoparticles in sun creams.
markScheme: Indicative content: advantages: better skin coverage; more effective protection from harmful UV light (reduces risk of sunburn and skin cancer); transparent so no white marks, so people may be more willing to use it; smaller quantities needed due to high surface area to volume ratio. Disadvantages: nanoparticles may be absorbed through the skin into the body; could damage cells; may be washed into the sea and harm marine organisms; long-term effects not yet known. Conclusion: a justified judgement, for example the protection from UV outweighs the possible risks, but more research is needed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least one advantage and one disadvantage, clearly explained, with a justified conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or more relevant points but one-sided, or no conclusion.
questions.explanation: Evaluation requires both sides and a conclusion. Linking advantages to small particle size and risks to absorption gains credit.

questions.question:
A company is deciding whether to use silver nanoparticles in sports socks to prevent odour.
Table 1 shows some information about silver nanoparticles.
Use the information in Table 1 and your knowledge of nanoparticles to evaluate whether the company should use silver nanoparticles.

rows: Silver nanoparticles kill bacteria that cause odour.
Mass of silver needed per pair of socks
0.1 g as nanoparticles; 2.0 g as silver thread
Up to half of the nanoparticles wash out after 10 washes.
Silver nanoparticles in waste water can kill bacteria used in sewage treatment.
The long-term effects of silver nanoparticles on human health are not yet known.

markScheme: Indicative content: advantages: antibacterial so odour reduced; high surface area to volume ratio so much more effective per gram; 0.1 g compared with 2.0 g, 20 times less silver needed, saving money and resources; disadvantages: half washes out after 10 washes so effect decreases over time; nanoparticles in waste water may kill bacteria in sewage treatment, damaging the treatment process and environment; small size means they may be absorbed through skin; long-term health effects unknown; conclusion: a justified decision, for example use them only after further testing, or do not use them because environmental risk outweighs benefit, or use them because so little silver is needed, with reasons.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed evaluation using the data (including the 20 times difference in mass and wash-out) and scientific knowledge (surface area to volume ratio, possible risks), weighing both sides to reach a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes advantages and disadvantages using some data, with a conclusion that is only partly justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple, mostly one-sided points copied from the information, with no clear conclusion.
questions.explanation: Top answers process the data (20 times less silver; 50% lost after 10 washes), link effectiveness to SA : V, explain risks, and finish with a reasoned decision.
